claims.text: Adding approximately 2 at.% Hf to nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 will suppress irradiation-induced Cr-V-rich precipitate formation near 8 dpa.
The Hf-modified alloy will preserve the baseline alloy's low-hardening behavior.
The Hf-modified alloy will preserve the baseline alloy's radiation resistance.
A 2 at.% Hf addition will maintain practical bulk manufacturability.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 can be produced by powder metallurgy, consolidation, and cold working or other severe-plastic-deformation processing.
Introducing Hf during powder preparation and consolidation can produce a homogeneous approximately 2 at.% Hf addition.
Hf atoms will segregate to grain boundaries, dislocations, or other defects during irradiation.
Segregated Hf will modify the local chemistry at potential precipitate-nucleation sites.
Hf will trap vacancies or alter solute-diffusion pathways that otherwise promote Cr-V-rich precipitation.
Hf acts as a kinetic inhibitor by capturing mobile irradiation defects and modifying solute interactions.
The Hf-induced changes in defect chemistry will reduce Cr and V clustering and thereby suppress precipitate nucleation and growth.
After irradiation, the Hf-modified alloy will have significantly fewer or nearly no Cr-V-rich precipitates relative to unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11.
After irradiation, the hardness of the Hf-modified alloy will be similar to or lower than that of the unmodified alloy.
TEM and XRD will show minimal secondary-phase formation in the irradiated Hf-modified alloy.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 forms Cr-V-rich precipitates under irradiation near 8 dpa.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 retains low hardening and reasonable radiation resistance near 8 dpa.
The proposed benefits apply up to 8 dpa within a specimen-temperature range of 300-400 °C.
Higher doses, temperatures outside 300-400 °C, or substantially higher Hf concentrations could produce unwanted phases or mechanical-property changes.
